extracted.intended_audience: plain TeX users, macro writers, and advanced TeX document authors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules, conventions, and idiomatic techniques for producing and debugging plain TeX documents, alignments, tables, displays, macros, and output routines. Focuses on how to format math and tables, write efficient macros, control boxes/leader behavior, and handle page/headline/footer routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \textstyle in multiline formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Switching to text style is especially common in multiline formulas. For example, you will probably find occasions to use \textstyle on both sides of the &’s within an \eqalign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 19.2 shows y = {1\over2}x in textstyle. Use \textstyle when you want smaller-style math in aligned/multiline contexts so vertical spacing and line breaks behave as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand difference between display math and formulas put in \hbox
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you type ‘$$\hbox{$\displaystyle{hformulai}$}$$’, the results are not quite the same: TEX will compress the glue in ‘$$hformulai$$’ if the formula is too wide to fit on a line at its natural width, but the glue inside \hbox{...} is frozen at its natural width. The \hbox version also invokes \everymath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t assume wrapping a \displaystyle formula in an \hbox produces identical behavior to a normal display; glue and breaking behavior differ, and \everymath is affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left-align a display by putting the formula in a full-line hbox
rubrics_metrics.description: One solution is to put the formula in an hbox that occupies a full line: $$\leftline{\indent$\displaystyle 1-{1\over2}+{1\over3}-{1\over4}+\cdots=\ln2$}$$
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To automate, define \leftdisplay and set \everydisplay{\leftdisplay} so you can type displays normally and have them left-aligned automatically. Note: this approach doesn’t work with equation numbers; Appendix D has methods to handle those.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asterisk in math mode is treated as a binary operation; fix spacing when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: When you type an asterisk in math mode, plain TEX considers * to be a binary operation. In ‘(*)’ and ‘(**)’ the binary operations are converted to type Ord, but the middle asterisk in ‘(***)’ remains of type Bin, giving ‘(∗ ∗ ∗)’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid the extra medium spaces, type ‘\eqno(*{*}*)’; or change \mathcode‘*’ if you never use * as a binary operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of equation numbers with \eqno and \leqno
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of \leqno, ‘(5)’ will appear flush left, followed by one quad of space in \textfont2, followed by one quad of space in the current text font, followed by ‘x = y’. With \eqno the widths will appear exactly 1 em from the left, and ‘(5)’ will appear flush right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the extra glue/quad spaces inserted with left-numbering; plan spacing if you need precise alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \smash{\raise...} to avoid increasing line height
rubrics_metrics.description: By raising the equation number, he increased the line height, so TEX put extra space between that line and the previous line when it calculated the inter-line glue. If he had said ‘\smash{\raise...}’, he wouldn’t have had that problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vertically moving symbols or numbers, wrap them in \smash if you don't want the box's height/depth to affect line spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of material inside an \eqalign box vs whole display
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘and’ occurs at the left of the \eqalign box, not at the left of the whole display, and the \eqalign box is centered as usual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't expect left-alignment of items inside an \eqalign to match the left edge of the enclosing display; \eqalign centers its box independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \llap (or \rlap) to position equation numbers within \displaylines
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: \displaylines{\hfill x\equiv x;\hfill\llap{(1)}\cr ... } creates left-numbered items using \llap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \llap to put numbers flush left inside a centered display without affecting the centering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \eqalignno / \leqalignno for aligned equations with equation numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Example shows \leqalignno{\gcd(u,v)&=\gcd(v,u);&(9)\cr \gcd(u,v)&=\gcd(-u,v).&(10)\cr}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These macros let you get aligned columns and attach equation numbers to individual lines; watch spacing quads to fine-tune number positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer copying a box for repeated identical content (efficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s much faster to copy a box than to build it up from scratch. For example, \setbox0=\vbox{...}% then \copy0 replicates processed content quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing many identical paragraphs (e.g., punishment example 100 times), prepare the paragraph once in a box (with struts if needed) and \copy it repeatedly to save processing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use struts to keep interbaseline distances correct when copying boxed paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: The struts in this example keep the interbaseline distances correct between boxed paragraphs, as explained in Chapter 12. Two struts are used, for if the message takes more than one line there will be a strut at both top and bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include invisible struts (zero-width boxes with specified height/depth) when copying multi-line boxes so baseline spacing remains consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ## when replacement text of a definition contains other definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The ## feature is indispensable when the replacement text of a definition contains other definitions. Example: \def\a#1{\def\b##1{##1#1}} after which ‘\a!’ expands to ‘\def\b#1{#1!}’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double the parameter-sign token in nested definition replacement text so parameters are recognized correctly at runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclose parameters in braces when passing parameters from one macro to another
rubrics_metrics.description: When you pass parameters from one macro to another in this way, you need to enclose them in braces as shown. Otherwise parameters can be copied multiple times and cost performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to pass parameters down into macros used repeatedly, consider defining control sequences to hold parameter values instead (faster) or ensure proper bracing to avoid misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \let vs \def carefully: \let captures current meaning, \def expands at use-time
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first case, \a receives the meaning of \b that is current at the time of the \let. In the second case, \a becomes a macro that will expand into the token \b whenever \a is used, so it has the meaning of \b that is current at the time of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose \let when you want to freeze the current meaning of a control sequence; use \def when you want delayed binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \expandafter / \edef tricks to control expansion order
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: \edef\next#1#2{\def#1{\b#2\d}} \next\a\c and other \edef/\expandafter combinations shown to manipulate expansion and token capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and use these expansion-control idioms when writing macros that must capture tokens/values at definition time vs use time; the appendix gives worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: You cannot define a macro that has unmatched braces
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s impossible to define a macro that has unmatched braces. But you can say \let\a={; Appendix D discusses several other brace tricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting to create definitions whose replacement text contains unmatched braces; TeX will read ahead to find the matching brace and you may get runaway definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle end-of-line (return) in \read by changing catcode or endlinechar or stripping space
rubrics_metrics.description: One way is to redefine \catcode‘\^^M=9 (ignored) just before the \read, so that the return will be ignored. Another solution is to redefine \endlinechar=-1, so that no character is put at the end of the line. Or you could try to strip off the space with macro expansion, with caveats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: the stripping macro approach fails if the user types ‘%’ at the end of the name or if the name contains control sequences. Prefer catcode or \endlinechar adjustments when safe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two safe ways to set \MYNAME from \myname and uppercase it
rubrics_metrics.description:
Solutions: \def
ext#1\endname{\uppercase{\def\MYNAME{#1}}} \expandafter
ext\myname\endname or \edef
ext{\def
oexpand\MYNAME{\myname}} \uppercase\expandafter{
ext}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these idioms to capture the content of a token list and apply \uppercase safely without unintended expansion side-effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number repetitions/lines in loops: use \endgraf as substitute for \par since \loop is not \long
rubrics_metrics.description: The only tricky part about this answer is the use of \endgraf, which is a substitute for \par because \loop is not a \long macro. Example provided that numbers lines in a \loop to verify number of repetitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \endgraf inside loops when paragraph breaks are needed; ensure constructs inside \loop are not expected to be \long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \leaders, \cleaders, \xleaders and \leaderfill idioms; prevent leader disappearance with \null\nobreak
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: \leaders: two boxes starting at 100 pt, 110 pt. \cleaders: three boxes starting at 95 pt, 105 pt, 115 pt. \xleaders: three boxes starting at 93 pt, 105 pt, 117 pt. Definition of \leaderfill shown. Use \null\nobreak to make sure the leaders do not disappear at a line break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate leader primitive for consistent tiling behavior; use \null\nobreak to stop leading material disappearing at page or line breaks; watch \parfillskip interaction (e.g., 'filll' glue).

rubrics_metrics.name: When copying boxed content, ensure appropriate glue handling (use struts and \null to preserve glue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The \null keeps glue (and leaders) from disappearing at the top of the page. Struts keep interbaseline distances correct between boxed paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine \null, \nobreak, and struts when assembling pages from box copies to preserve intended spacing and to avoid lost leaders at breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \smallskip to separate table heading and footing from the table; use \negthinspace for italic correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice the uses of ‘\smallskip’ here to separate the table heading and footing from the table itself; such refinements are often worthwhile. The ‘\negthinspace’ in the title line is a small backspace that compensates for the slant in an italic W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply small vertical spacing commands for better table aesthetics and use small horizontal adjustments (\negthinspace) to correct italic slant artifacts observed on proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set multiletter identifiers in text italics, and reset tabs with \cleartabs when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiletter identifiers look best when set in text italics with \it. In such programs it seems best to type \cleartabs just before &, whenever it is desirable to reset the old tabs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When typesetting algorithms or code in tables, use text italics for identifiers and explicitly reset tab positions if the tabbing state has to change within the program listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \halign preambles and \tabskip glue to center and space equation parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The equation is divided into separate parts for terms and plus/minus signs, and tabskip glue is used to center it: example uses \openup1\jot \tabskip=0pt plus1fil \halign to\displaywidth{... \tabskip=0pt plus1fil & ...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the \halign preamble with appropriate \tabskip settings to distribute space across columns (e.g., center parts of long displayed systems of equations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \pmatrix and \multispan/bigstrut tricks for matrices and improved table title spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: \pmatrix{a_{11}&a_{12}&\ldots&a_{1n}\cr ...}. For table title spacing include lines with ‘\omit&height2pt&\multispan5&\cr’ or put \bigstrut into a column of the title line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \pmatrix for matrix displays; for better-looking table title lines add invisible struts or extra rows to give the title breathing room and avoid cramped rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empty extreme columns to let \hrulefill span tabskip glue
rubrics_metrics.description: The trick is to have “empty” columns at the extreme left and right; then the \hrulefill’s are able to span the tabskip glue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing decorative rules across a table, reserve left/right empty columns so the fill glue can stretch and the rules align as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \valign to transpose rows and columns
rubrics_metrics.description: With \valign transposes rows and columns, the result is used to solve Dudeney's pennies problem by arranging macros \one and \two in a \valign so rows become columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you need to transpose a grid of boxes, consider \valign rather than building the transposed table by hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customize \output routine, headlines, and footlines for multi-column and special page formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: \footline={...}, \headline={...}, \output={\plainoutput\blankpageoutput} and a triplecolumn output routine that collects column boxes in \leftcolumn, \midcolumn, etc., then shipout with \fullline{\box\leftcolumn\hfil\box\midcolumn\hfil\columnbox}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble output routines carefully: set \hsize appropriate for columns, manage \outputpenalty and \supereject, and at the end flush any remaining column boxes to avoid lost material. The appendix provides a full pattern for triple-column formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put marks and insertions after boxes to avoid breakpoints; use \nobreak after \mark when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: He forgot that interline glue is inserted automatically before the \leftline; this permits a legal breakpoint between the \mark and the \leftline box. One cure would be to say \nobreak just after the \mark; but it’s usually best to put marks and insertions just after boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing \mark or insertion primitives in positions that allow legal breaks; place them immediately after box material or guard them with \nobreak to keep page layout stable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure index continuation lines fit in \vsize to avoid infinite loops
rubrics_metrics.description: If the text of the main and/or subsidiary entry is lengthy, a continuation line may actually become two or more lines. The \vsize must be large enough to accommodate all continuation lines plus at least one more line of index material, or else infinite looping will occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building index/continuation lines inside an \output routine, check that page body dimensions accommodate expected continuation material to prevent runaway page-building loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: \meaning of \chardef/\mathchardef uses hexadecimal notation; be aware of category code consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If \cs has been defined by \chardef or \mathchardef, TEX uses hexadecimal notation when it expands \meaning\cs, and it assigns category 12 to each digit of the expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parsing or displaying definitions created by \chardef/\mathchardef, remember their expansion uses hex notation and digits will have 'other' category codes; watch for situations where you want digits treated as numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know numeric limits and table sizes (register limits, dimension limits, badness conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: There are 256 possible characters, hence 256 entries in each of the \catcode, \mathcode, \lccode, etc. tables. There are 256 \box registers, 256 \count registers, 256 \dimen registers, etc. A \dimeni value must be less than 2^30 sp in absolute value; a \hnumberi must be less than 2^31 in absolute value. Badness ratings, penalties, and INITEX defaults (e.g., \tolerance initialized to 10000) are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these numeric and table limits to design macros that won't overflow registers or violate constraints; consult these bounds when debugging bizarre arithmetic or allocation errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debugging Missing number and other errors: use \tracingcommands / \tracingmacros
rubrics_metrics.description: If you get a ‘Missing number’ error and you can’t guess why TEX is looking for a number, plant the instruction ‘\tracingcommands=1’ shortly before the error point; your log file will show what command TEX is working on. Also illustrate \tracingmacros=1 for expansion traces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with cryptic errors, enable the appropriate tracing parameter to see the command currently being executed or the macro-expansion trace; this often reveals the cause quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use input tricks to recover after an error (interactive editing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When TEX reports an error, you can delete unwanted tokens then insert what you want: Type ‘6’ and then ‘I\macro’. There are sneaky ways to get at \inaccessible control sequences by typing 'I\garbage{}\let\accessible=' in response to an error prompt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interactive fixes at the error prompt allow token deletion/insertion; some tricks exist to recover otherwise inaccessible control sequences but use them carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: If stuck, look up the answer but try first to solve it yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can’t solve a problem, you can always look up the answer. But please, try first to solve it by yourself; then you’ll learn more and you’ll learn faster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaguideline: attempt to understand and solve TeX problems before consulting sources to maximize learning; use the appendix and index after reasonable effort.
